Le système judiciaire : un fardeau de pl: The justice system: one more burden for women who are victims of domestic violence
Le juge de la cour familiale doit mainte: Family court judges must now look into the decisions of other courts.
Nous sommes le dimanche 21 février à Lav: It is Sunday, February 21, in Laval. Dawn is still pale when Marly Édouard is found lifeless. She was a radio host, and she was 32. Two days earlier, on Friday the 19th, she had called the police after receiving death threats from her partner’s ex. The police came, met with her and left. Her complaint was never followed up. But the threat was very real. Four other femicides have taken place in the past two weeks.
Nancy Roy a été tuée par son compagnon à: Nancy Roy was killed by her partner in Saint-Hyacinthe, Elisapee Angma by her ex in Kuujjuaq, and Myriam Dallaire and Sylvie Bisson by Myriam’s violent partner in Sainte-Sophie. On International Women’s Rights Day, it bears repeating that 78% of victims of domestic violence are women. That figure is no coincidence. “Despite the progress made on the issue, many people still largely believe that domestic violence is a matter of isolated cases or accidents,” says Louise Riendeau, policy coordinator at the Regroupement des maisons pour femmes victimes de violence conjugale.
Cette violence est en fait le signe que: This violence is in fact a sign that inequalities between men and women persist.” For victims and survivors of domestic violence, it is the entire system that needs to change.
Béatrice* s’est séparée de son ancien co: Béatrice* separated from her former partner in February 2015, after years of domestic violence. The entire legal process ended in December 2020. For her, those five years were exhausting and very costly. Like many women who are victims of domestic violence, she was in a state of post-traumatic shock throughout the process. “We [victims] carry the burden of proof, when we don’t have the means to. You really have to be sharp and play detective. It’s up to the woman to do everything,” she says indignantly, describing the “painstaking work” she did to gather evidence to prove that her story was true.
Et le nombre de défaillances auxquelles: And the number of failures she faced is hard to sum up. Youth protection workers from the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ) regularly questioned her version of events and told her: “It’s up to you to protect your child. If your child is afraid and doesn’t want to sleep at their father’s, maybe you’re the cause.”
Son avocate en droit de la famille ne l’: Her family lawyer didn’t listen to her: “The judge won’t believe you; it’s your word against the father’s.” For Béatrice, all of this reveals “a numbness toward domestic violence.”
Nous sommes en décembre 2020. Les procès: It is December 2020. The trials are over, the verdicts have come down, but Béatrice is desperate. “I finally got heard, but my child didn’t,” she says, helpless. The family court granted the father custody of their daughter two weekends out of three, plus visitation on Wednesday evenings. Yet at the end of the criminal trial, the man was found guilty of criminal harassment, since there is no crime of domestic violence.
Il lui était depuis interdit de contacte: He has since been prohibited from contacting the mother and daughter. But the criminal and family courts don’t communicate with each other, which Béatrice finds absurd and frustrating. To comply with the family court’s judgment and the father’s wishes, she still lives in the same village as her former partner. “Today, my ex still has a hold over me through my child,” she says. Her daughter is the very person she wanted to protect. With horror and despair, she tells us how deeply her child has been marked by the domestic violence that broke up the family. “She has an anxiety disorder, has problems at school and doesn’t speak.
Elle a aussi un trouble de l’attachement: She also has an attachment disorder, she blocks her emotions.” According to the child’s psychologist, these problems risk becoming irreversible if she keeps going to her father’s. Paralyzed by the family court’s judgment, Béatrice keeps sending her daughter to her father’s. To her, it feels as if she were trivializing the violence. “I’m giving her the message that ‘it’s okay, sweetie, you can go,’” she says, emotional.
Dans un dernier élan d’espoir, déterminé: In one last surge of hope, determined to protect her daughter, she sent her story to about thirty members of the federal and provincial governments and to four media outlets. She wrote an 11-page text and recorded a 30-minute podcast. Her message in a bottle got a few sympathetic replies promising action, but she is still waiting.
Pour tenter de corriger ces lacunes, le: In an attempt to correct these shortcomings, the expert committee tasked with improving support for victims of sexual assault and domestic violence published a <l1>report</l1> in December 2020. Among its 190 proposals is the creation of a specialized court for sexual assault and domestic violence. On <l2>February 8</l2>, Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette set up a working group to establish this new body. Béatrice welcomes the idea, even though she is “waiting to see.” In her view, the report contains some interesting elements, but she finds it incomplete.
« C’est super pour les victimes actuelle: “That’s great for current victims, but what about those experiencing post-separation violence, or the children?” she asks. Indeed, the two trials she went through did not change the father’s life, while the lives of Béatrice and her daughter will never be the same. For now, Béatrice has no recourse. “I’m afraid the father will renegotiate the agreement. If I go back to court, I can’t use the evidence that was used in the other judgments. That scares me,” she explains. With a daughter who doesn’t speak and evidence she can no longer use, the mother feels stuck in a dead end.
« On perpétue la violence de génération: “We perpetuate violence from generation to generation, hoping it will change,” observes Béatrice. Indeed, more than one in five victims of domestic violence witnessed it during their childhood, according to the most recent <l1>data</l1> from Statistics Canada.
Depuis le 1er mars, une nouvelle Loi sur: Since March 1, a new Divorce Act could change the game in Quebec. Family court judges must now look into the decisions of other courts. In addition, psychological domestic violence is now taken into account. “We’ve been talking about the inconsistency between courts for years. We hope this law will change that,” says Louise Riendeau. “For now it only applies to married couples, but it’s already encouraging,” the coordinator adds. Judges and lawyers still need to be made aware of these issues in order to apply these measures.
Par ailleurs, Mme Riendeau reproche au s: Ms. Riendeau also criticizes the justice system for not recognizing everything as domestic violence. “Not all assaults are recognized as punishable offences, even though they can do much more harm to women,” she laments. In cases of harassment, for example, there must have been several incidents before the offence is taken into account.
Il est par ailleurs nécessaire de rappel: It also needs to be said that, beyond the laws, domestic violence is still surrounded by stubborn stereotypes. “Even though the consequences of violence on children have been shown, people still think it stops after the separation,” says Ms. Riendeau. These preconceptions persist among youth protection workers, lawyers and police officers as well. And they influence how victims are dealt with and supported, she says.
« Bien qu’on en parle depuis plus de 40: “Even though we’ve been talking about it for more than 40 years, the link between domestic violence and patriarchy isn’t always made. People will think it’s an isolated incident, that it’s someone with a mental health problem,” she continues. The coordinator believes this is a problem and that we must keep talking about it and making that link. “The lack of equality between men and women is why it keeps happening,” she adds.
Anne* a vécu deux ans avec un conjoint v: Anne* lived for two years with a violent partner. She managed to leave after he strangled her. It took her several days to sign her complaint, because she didn’t want to “harm him.” The case was postponed many times, and the trial was finally held in February 2021. As in many cases, he pleaded guilty and was convicted.
Il a obtenu une absolution inconditionne: He received an absolute discharge and was given no psychological follow-up. Anne is neither surprised nor disappointed: “I’m tired, I was just waiting for him to be found guilty, because I can’t forget that evening when he strangled me.” To ensure her protection after the breakup, Anne had to buy a surveillance camera and have her computer checked to protect her accounts and information. “I got an order that he can’t come onto my street or contact me directly or indirectly,” she explains. Because she still lives in the same village as him, she has regularly found herself face to face with her abuser, despite the order.
« Je l’ai vu deux fois l’été passé, car: “I saw him twice last summer, because our kids go to the same day camp. Both times, he parked right in front of me. He never got out of the car,” she recalls. Anne is far from the only one for whom a no-contact order isn’t enough to guarantee her safety. It is common for such orders to be neither respected nor monitored, as a <l1>research report</l1> published in November 2020 denounced.
« Le ministère de la Sécurité publique m: “The Ministère de la Sécurité publique will also conduct a feasibility study on the implementation of anti-approach bracelets as a means of preventing domestic homicides,” wrote Paul-Jean Charest, spokesperson for the Ministère de la Justice, in an email to us. He was careful to add, however, that “for the protection to be effective, complainants must report breaches so that charges can be laid.”

Pour pallier toutes ces lacunes, le rapp: To address all these shortcomings, the expert committee’s report published last December proposes increasing the number of prosecutors, but also training the various people involved in domestic violence cases. For Louise Riendeau, this training would allow them to detect domestic violence, even in actions that seem the most caring.
« Pour ce qui est de la violence conjuga: “When it comes to domestic violence, a situation we see a lot is when the violent partner buys all of his wife’s clothes. It looks charming, but when you know the subject, you know it’s a way of controlling what she wears,” she says. Support workers at shelters for women who are victims of domestic violence have a major role to play here: “We need to use their expertise to train people at the DPJ and police officers, and to work on risk assessment.”
Les intervenantes assument en effet un r: Support workers indeed play an essential role in these women’s lives. Béatrice believes that without them, she would have dropped her case. “If all of this is done, it could be less of a burden for the victim,” Ms. Riendeau hopes. She believes the government is at a “pivotal moment” and must take up the issue. The survivors we met all live in the hope that political decision-makers will open their eyes to the situation.
« Regardons comment cela se passe pour l: “Let’s look at how it goes for victims! Let’s look at the consequences for our children,” says Béatrice. In the meantime, women continue to die from the consequences of domestic violence. In the meantime, Béatrice’s daughter continues to carry the burden of domestic violence on her child’s shoulders. And celebrating International Women’s Rights Day won’t be enough to bring them justice. “Things have to move,” chant those who are still alive. * The names of these women have been changed to respect their anonymity.

« Il faut le même accès à la justice par: “We need the same access to justice everywhere in Quebec, not just in big centres,” says Louise Riendeau. The numbers speak for themselves: women living in the regions are at higher risk. According to the most recent <l1>data</l1> from the Ministère de la Sécurité publique, the Côte-Nord has the highest rate of offences against the person in a domestic context. In 2015, the region recorded 590 offences per 100,000 population. The provincial average is 269 offences per 100,000 population.
Le <l1>premier rapport annuel du Comité: The <l1>first annual report of the Domestic Violence Death Review Committee</l1> was made public in December 2020. It recommends that people involved in domestic violence cases be trained, that the public be made aware, and that tools be developed for police.
Le projet de loi C-247 propose d’ajouter: Bill C-247 proposes adding the crime of “controlling or coercive conduct” to the Criminal Code. The proposal refers to “coercive control,” a crucial concept in domestic violence that still struggles to gain recognition. Coercive control, which covers threats, belittling, surveillance or isolation, all the small stratagems that keep fear and a hold over a partner in place, has been criminalized in English law since 2015. Passing Bill C-247 would make it possible to recognize and criminalize domestic violence other than physical or sexual violence.
